comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Done. The coalescing moved into Sources/MusterMac/LatestRequestSender.swift and both callers keep only what they genuinely do differently - the find bar drops an answer to a needle already typed past, the divider drops all of them. Reading a refusal out of a response moved with it, since both did that identically too.

Worth recording why the old comment argued against this, since it was wrong in an instructive way: it said merging would hand the divider a callback it has no use for. That reads the split in the wrong place. What differs is the answer type and what is done with it, which a generic and a closure cover; what is the same is the interleaving of the pending request and the in-flight flag across a hop off the main thread and back - the subtle part, and the part a change would otherwise have to be made in twice.

Covered by the two tests that already existed: 'a needle reaches the core, and only the last one typed does', and 'a drag sends the position the pointer reached, not every one it passed'.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
`SplitRatioSender` (divider drags) and `FindSender` (find keystrokes) each implement the same shape independently: one request in flight, the latest input remembered, and the last one always sent. Both exist because the same problem showed up twice - a per-event round trip over a forwarded socket is tens of milliseconds a keystroke.

They were left apart deliberately rather than by oversight. The find work would have had to widen into a file another parallel slot was editing, and the two are not actually identical: `FindSender` carries an answer back to draw, `SplitRatioSender` has nothing to return. That difference is the design question a shared version has to answer.

Worth lifting when a third one appears - three examples say what the shape really is, where two can only be guessed at.
title: ♻️ Two senders keep one request in flight, and share no code
